I'm considering a noise model instead of a shift: treating test margins as the in-sample signed margins plus random Gaussian noise, with the noise scale chosen so that about 22.5% come out negative. That feels like a reasonable picture of how fine-tuning overfit might show up on unseen items, so I'll compute both the shift and noise versions to compare.

idx=np.arange(1000)
oth = BL.copy(); oth[idx,y] = -np.inf
sm = BL[idx,y] - oth.max(1)
print('in-sample signed margin <0:', np.mean(sm<0))
# calibrate shift
from scipy.optimize import brentq
delta = brentq(lambda d: np.mean(sm-d<0)-0.225, 0, 5); print('shift delta', delta)
rng=np.random.default_rng(1)
def frac_neg_tau(t):
    return np.mean((sm[None,:]+t*np.random.default_rng(5).standard_normal((200,1000)))<0)
tau = brentq(lambda t: frac_neg_tau(t)-0.225, 0.01, 10); print('tau', tau)
def noise(L):
    # noise on (true - best other) direction per item using item's own runner-up: approximate via base top/runner-up margin noise
    dm=L-BL; top=bp; ru=np.argsort(BL,1)[:,-2]
    return dm[idx,top]-dm[idx,ru]
variants = {'m2048old':np.load('pass_12/logits.npy'), 'm1536v2':np.load('lg_m1536_v2.npy'), 'm1536old':np.load('pass_10/logits.npy')}
for model in ['shift','tau']:
    for name,L in variants.items():
        nm = noise(L); losses=[]
        for t in range(3000):
            j = rng.integers(0,1000,400)
            s_t = sm[j]-delta if model=='shift' else sm[j]+tau*rng.standard_normal(400)
            n = rng.choice(nm,400)*rng.choice([-1,1],400)
            new = s_t + n
            broken = ((s_t>0)&(new<0)).sum(); fixed = ((s_t<0)&(new>0)).sum()
            losses.append(broken-fixed)
        losses=np.array(losses)
        print(f'{model} {name}: mean {losses.mean():.2f} sd {losses.std():.2f} P(loss>4) {np.mean(losses>4):.3f}  P(>3) {np.mean(losses>3):.3f}')
